 Psychology explains why some people feel calmer on rainy days while others feel low or restless; what our responses to weather reveal about mood, memories and our surroundings

 Medium

 Print (Image Credit: Canva) For some people rainy days feel like a peek into heaven, with the smell of mud and a hot cup of tea to cosy up with. But for others it can feel like their worst nightmare where they feel low and restless. Psychology suggests that there could be fascinating connections between personal memories and our reaction to our surroundings. Some people take the first raindrops as an invitation to slow down. Their coffee machine gets active, their favourite playlist begins, and suddenly the world outside the window looks like a scene from Wake Up Sid (2009). However others can feel the complete opposite. Incoming rain can bring a restless afternoon, low mood and cancelled plans because they better just stay home. Interestingly, neither reaction is unusual. Rain has a peculiar way of changing the atmosphere around us, quite literally and emotionally. It alters the light, changes familiar sounds, brings a distinct smell to the air and often forces us to rearrange our plans. Yet, while one person finds comfort in this temporary pause, another may feel trapped by it. Psychology suggests that our responses to rainy weather are shaped by several overlapping influences, including our surroundings, memories, daily routines and individual sensitivity to changes in the environment. In other words, we may all be watching the same clouds gather, but we are not necessarily experiencing the same day. The soothing side of a rainy afternoon
 There is a reason why the sound of rain features so frequently in sleep playlists, meditation recordings and cosy café soundtracks. Its steady rhythm can create a soothing background, especially when it replaces louder, unpredictable sounds from the outside world. Imagine sitting beside a window while rain taps against the glass. There is no expectation to go for a walk, no pressure to make the most of a sunny afternoon and perhaps no guilt about spending an hour doing absolutely nothing. The weather appears to give you permission to pause. There is scientific interest in this connection, too. A 2024 systematic review titled “ The effect of exposure to natural sounds on stress reduction: a systematic review and meta-analysis ” found that exposure to natural sounds was associated with differences in physiological measures such as heart rate, blood pressure and breathing rate compared with quiet environments. The research examined natural sounds broadly, rather than rain alone, so it does not prove that rainfall will calm everyone. Still, it offers a useful clue about why the soundscape of a rainy day can feel restorative. For some, rain is not gloomy at all. It is nature turning down the volume. When grey skies bring the mood down
 Now consider the other side of the window. You have plans to meet a friend, traffic is already a nightmare, your shoes are getting wet, and the sky looks as though someone has turned down the brightness on the entire city. In this situation, rain does not sound like a relaxing soundtrack. It becomes an obstacle. (Image Credit: Canva) One important explanation lies in the way weather changes our routines. Rain can mean cancelled outings, longer commutes, less time outdoors and fewer spontaneous encounters. If your favourite way to unwind involves a morning walk, a game of badminton or coffee with friends at an outdoor café, a rainy spell can take away some of the activities that usually lift your mood. Light matters, too. Grey skies reduce the amount of natural daylight available, which can affect how people feel thropughout the day. A 2005 study titled " A Warm Heart and a Clear Head: The Contingent Effects of Weather on Mood and Cognition ", found that weather's relationship with mood depended on factors such as the season and how much time participants spent outdoors. So, if a rainy afternoon leaves you feeling lazy and unproductive, it does not necessarily mean you dislike rain itself. You may simply miss the daylight, movement and freedom that a clear day makes easier. Rain, memories and the places we call home
 Another feeling that is associated with a rainy day is the one with home. Have you ever caught the smell of wet earth and suddenly remembered school holidays at your grandparents' house? Perhaps the sound of rain against a tin roof reminds you of childhood evenings, hot pakoras and family conversations that seemed to last forever. (Image Credit: canva) For many people in India, the monsoon arrives carrying an entire collection of sensory memories. There is the smell of the mud after rain, a clear sky after a hot summer day and the sight of children rejoicing in rain. These associations can shape how we feel when the clouds gather. If rainy weather has always been connected with comfort, family time or travel for you, your mind is most probable to associate it with pleasant experiences. But, if it reminds you of lonely evenings, difficult journeys or disrupted plans, the same weather may evoke less comforting feelings. This becomes an explanation for how your experiences through the years in different weathers can shape your feelings towards it today. Of course, a rainy day does not automatically unlock a particular memory, and personal associations are difficult to separate from other influences. But the broader idea is compelling. We do not experience the environment as a collection of neutral sights and sounds; we experience it through the meaning we have attached to it.
